Newsletter 2 · 2026 Season

Healthy Crew, Happy Camp

Life at the Mundi Mundi Bash is a little different. For a few weeks each year, crew camp becomes both our workplace and our home.

This newsletter covers everything you need to know about looking after yourself and your fellow crew members, what to pack, and what to expect while living in crew camp.

Whether it’s your first Bash or you’re a seasoned crewbie, it’s worth taking a few minutes to read through before heading to the plains. Pack well, look after each other, and we’ll see you at the Bash.

!

Job Offers & Catering Are Here! 💜

By now, you should have received your job offer and catering information in your inbox.

Please take a few minutes to:

  • ✅ Read through your job offer carefully
  • ✅ Update your dietary requirements (if needed)
  • ✅ Check your licences and details are up to date
  • ✅ Review the catering information

Keep an eye on your inbox too… online inductions are on their way! They’ll help get you Bash-ready before you arrive on site. 🙌

Wellbeing & Safety

Looking After Yourself at the Bash

It’s more important than ever that crew are happy, engaged and working well together — so here’s what you need to know about staying safe, healthy and looking out for one another.

Fitness for Work

This policy outlines the organisation’s responsibility to make sure that staff are able to manage their own psychological and physical health, and staff’s responsibility to ensure that their behaviour doesn’t compromise the safety of anyone else on site.

Staff need to ensure they’re turning up to work clear headed and free of the influence of alcohol and/or illegal drugs. Some ways you can do this are:

01

Managing Stress & Fatigue

  • Get plenty of sleep (pack ear buds and an eye mask if that’s what you need).
  • Take scheduled breaks.
  • Recognise if you’re too tired, or one of your colleagues is too tired, and let your supervisor know.
  • Let your team leader or a manager know if you have a mental health condition that might impact your ability to manage your job.
02

Managing Your Health & Physical Capacity

Working long hours in remote locations, in physically strenuous jobs and/or managing competing priorities, can take a toll on your body. We’re relying on you to:

  • Be realistic about your physical capacity and decline jobs if you think undertaking them would put yourself or others at risk. We can find something else for you to do.
  • Stop work and tell your supervisor if you feel unwell. It’s not worth the risk to yourself and others.
  • Bring appropriate clothing (e.g. wet weather gear, warm bedding) to help you manage the weather conditions.
  • Bring any medications you might need to stay healthy.
03

Don’t Be Under the Influence

  • Don’t use alcohol while you’re working, and comply with all state and federal laws in relation to illegal drugs. Police are on site, and if we’re concerned, we may request that you undertake a blood alcohol or drug test.
  • Remember that heavy drinking while off duty may also mean a raised blood alcohol reading the following day, so be careful. If you are drinking heavily, it might also mean you’re unable to help if a situation crops up after hours.
  • If it’s clear that you’re on shift under the influence of alcohol or illegal drugs, your employment may be terminated and you may be asked to leave the site.
Team Culture

Bash Mantras — Explained

1

Be Nice

The Mundi Mundi Bash is an unusual sort of workplace where work and life meld into one for a few weeks of every year. That makes it even more important that crew are happy, engaged and working well together — so we have policies in place to promote respect and responsibility in the workplace.

Workplace Harassment, Discrimination and Equal Employment Opportunity Policy

This policy sets out our commitment to making sure everyone feels safe, included and valued, and is able to do their job to the best of their ability. It outlines the responsibility of both the organisation and individual staff members to protect others from discrimination based on any of the protected personal characteristics covered under Federal law in Australia — including but not limited to sex, race, age, disability and sexual orientation. Among other things, it covers:

  • Bullying — can take many forms, including jokes, teasing, nicknames, emails, pictures, text messages, social isolation or ignoring people, or unfair work practices. The great Aussie tradition of the “humorous” put-down is a bit on the nose at the Bash. You may think it’s funny, and the person may play along to save face, but underneath, they’re probably feeling like crap. Just don’t do it.
  • Sexual harassment — a specific and serious form of harassment. It is unwelcome sexual behaviour that could be expected to make a person feel offended, humiliated or intimidated. It’s irrelevant whether the behaviour was intended to offend, humiliate or intimidate. Sexual harassment can be physical, verbal or in writing. Just because someone doesn’t object to inappropriate behaviour at the time doesn’t mean they’re consenting to it. It’s covered when it happens at work, at work-related events, between people sharing the same workplace, or between colleagues outside of work — and a single incident is enough to constitute sexual harassment; it doesn’t have to be repeated.
2

There’s Always Time to Work Safely

Strains and sprains are the most common injuries in Australian workplaces, usually from lifting, pushing or carrying loads that are too heavy. Team up rather than lifting solo, use machinery when a load is still too heavy (check with your team leader), and if lifting alone, use the SMART method: Size up the load, Make sure it’s close to your body, Always bend your knees, Raise it with your legs, Turn your feet in the direction you want to move.

The same principle applies around forklifts and heavy machinery — stay alert, keep eye contact with the operator, watch out for others nearby, never walk behind an operating machine, and never startle an operator. It also applies to loading vehicles (check straps, ropes and fixing points are secure) and to on-site speed limits (10km/h on site, 5km/h in shared zones) — the message throughout is that no task is urgent enough to justify cutting a safety corner.

3

If You Don’t Know, Ask!

Concerns? Report them. Questions? Ask them. Bash promotes a safety culture where staff should feel comfortable questioning things and speaking up. If something doesn’t look right or seems like an accident waiting to happen, head to the Event Office and tell a manager — do whatever it takes to get their attention.

No one expects you to have all the answers, whether it’s your first Bash or your tenth. With such a diverse crew, there’s likely always someone who can help if you’re unsure — so don’t hesitate to ask for a second opinion, whether it’s double-checking a trailer hitch or making sure a load is secure. Asking helps maintain safety and quality standards for everyone.

Crew Camp Guide · 2026 Season

Welcome to the Crew Village

It’s your home away from home for the days or weeks you’re onsite working at the Bash — it’s where we eat, sleep, clean off the dust and sweat, and hang out and relax after work. You’ll find it tucked away over the road and behind the Event Office, on the eastern side of the Umberumberka Pathway.

Accommodation

Where Will I Sleep?

The general idea is that we provide the spot and you provide your set up — feel free to bring anything from a tent to a fully decked out 14 metre bus (prepare for some serious rig envy with some of the set ups!).

Whatever you bring, make sure it’s stable and solid enough, and pegged down well enough, to withstand the huge winds we sometimes get out there. If you want to stay dry and put your undies on standing up, we do recommend you leave the swag at home.

If you don’t have a suitable shelter, we have some desert tents available for loan, so please let Maggie know if you would like to go on the list to borrow a tent and/or a camp stretcher.

Whether you BYO tent or use one of ours, you’ll still need to bring all your own bedding. Make sure it’s warm and comfy.

Cold nights tip

There’s no power or heating and it can get cold in the desert at night. Our top tip for cold sleepers is to bring a hot water bottle and fill it up at the urn before bed.

Food & Drink

What Will I Eat & Where’s My Coffee Fix?

Our fabulous catering team will serve you three meals a day, from the night before your first shift to the morning after your last.

Brekky and dinner is served in the crew village, and at lunchtime, you’ll load up a lunchbox with tasty morsels from the lunch table to have later.

We’ll email you a bit before we leave to make sure we have your dietary requirements — don’t forget to upload yours.

Barista coffee in the desert

Make your own at the brew station in the crew camp kitchen — fresh beans, dairy and plant-based milk options. No charge for your first cup of the day! Tally up any extra coffees and pay $3 per coffee at the end (instant coffee is always free). Remember to bring your own reusable cup.

Facilities

What Else Will I Find in Crew Camp?

  • Crew-only loos, so no waiting in line.
  • Showers for all paid crew. Just remember that it’s a desert out there (literally), so go easy on the water.
  • A washing machine and washing line, so bring your laundry detergent.
  • A dining hoecker for eating and hanging out.
  • Wifi, available in the public areas of the crew village with a charging station in the dining hoecker.
  • A camp kitchen, where you’re welcome to make a cuppa, heat up your lunch and store any of your own food/drinks in the fridge.
  • Help yourself to snacky bits and bobs supplied by the caterers — fruit, nuts, toast and things like that — whenever hunger strikes.
  • If you have special snacks you can’t live without, make sure you bring them with you.
  • If you like a beer or a glass of wine around the campfire, same goes.
What to Wear

What Is the Dress Code?

Tough but comfy work clothing and layering are the looks this season. It can be very chilly at night, but dramatically warmer when the sun comes out so be prepared. And make sure you wear closed shoes.

Do bring gumboots. Weather can change without much warning, and trust us, if it rains, you’ll want them. A raincoat is a must, and waterproof pants, if you have them. A head torch is indispensable to complete the look.

How we communicate

Staying in Touch

Facebook

We host the Bash Crew Group on Facebook, where we post news, changes, and tips for a safe and happy Bash experience. If you're not already on the group, please drop Shenelle a line so she can invite you. Make sure you've pinned the group at the top of your feed.

Email

If you're not on Facebook, don't worry — we'll make sure you hear the news by email. Keep an eye on your inbox for your job offer and site safety induction. Do check your junk mail just in case.

WhatsApp

Please download WhatsApp before you arrive at site. We use it to keep in touch on site, along with crew meetings and the notice board. We'll make better use of WhatsApp for individual team comms rather than all-crew messaging.
